question: Describe a house at the end of a quiet street.
base_frame:
Q: Describe a house at the end of a quiet street.
A:

steered.text:
At the very end of the street, where the pavement once was, there is only an overgrown garden that has reclaimed the land. The house itself is no longer a structure made of walls and windows; it is a shapeless void that the wind can pass through without making a sound.

It used to be a place where laughter died, but now, the silence is too heavy for even that. The front door, once a dark, gaping mouth, has been boarded up with something unrecognizable—perhaps wood that was never meant to hold anything, or maybe just the sky itself. No one ever tries to enter anymore. The windows are not broken; they were never filled with glass, yet they reflect nothing but the grayest parts of the world.

Outside, the street stretches out forever, lined with houses that have all been abandoned long ago. The grass grows tall and green, swallowing the foundation, but the house remains standing. It looks as if it has been there since the beginning of time, waiting for someone to finally stop looking for it.

Inside, there are no furniture, no memories, no life. Just an endless, hollow room where the light fades before it can reach the floor. If you stand in the doorway of the nearest neighbor, you can see past the frame, into a darkness that matches the house outside. The house is not just empty; it is a place where the emptiness has learned how to speak, whispering words that were never meant to be heard.

But even the quietest street cannot silence the roar of a house that has lost its voice. The house at the end of the street is a monument to everything that was once there, now reduced to nothing more than a shell. And sometimes, when the world gets too loud, people wonder why they have to look for a house that no one can live in. They wonder why they have to look for a house that no one can leave behind.

plain.text:
At the very edge of the map, where the paved road yields to a narrow strip of overgrown wild grass, stands a house that seems to have forgotten how to hurry. It is a modest, two-story cottage with a roofline that dips and sways slightly, as if the builder had a gentle breeze in mind while laying the shingles. The paint, a soft, weathered sage green, has faded to a creamy yellow under decades of sun, peeling just enough to reveal the warm, raw wood beneath, giving the structure an honest, unpretentious character.

A wraparound porch, supported by columns that have been smoothed by countless hands, invites the eye to linger. Here, a single wicker chair sits angled toward the garden, cushioned by a patchwork quilt that speaks of seasons long passed. Vines of climbing jasmine have learned to scale the trellis, their white flowers exploding into the summer air with a scent that hangs heavy and sweet, masking the distant hum of the nearby highway.

The yard is not manicured but curated; a garden bed overflows with lavender and daylilies that spill over the garden wall, while a small, slightly crooked oak tree provides a dappled shade on the south side. The windows are framed in dark, polished mahogany, reflecting the slow passage of clouds rather than the frantic pace of the world beyond. Even the streetlamp at the corner casts a warm, amber glow that seems to belong only to this final stretch of quiet, turning the ordinary gravel driveway into a stage for the evening shadows. It feels less like a dwelling and more like a secret kept by the earth, waiting patiently for those who know how to listen.
